operationalization: Compare clutch size of raptor species with that of other birds of similar body size, and check that the kestrel has the largest raptor clutch; the claim is refuted if raptors lay as many eggs as comparable non-raptors or other raptors exceed the kestrel.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size by species, to rank raptors against other birds

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET: morphological, ecological and geographical data for all birds
candidate_datasets.role: body mass to control for size

obstacles: 'Unprolific' is relative and needs a body-size comparison
Other raptors such as some owls and falcons may rival the kestrel clutch
rationale: Clutch size is among the best-documented avian traits and raptors are easy to identify, so the comparison can be run directly. The kestrel exception makes the claim sharp enough to refute.

operationalization: Score nest construction for every incubating bird species and check whether the hoopoe alone has none; any other species laying in a bare cavity without nest material refutes the 'only' claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of nest type and nest-site for the hoopoe and for cavity or ground nesters

obstacles: 'No nest at all' is a threshold: hoopoes use a cavity with some debris, nightjars lay on bare ground
No single trait database records nest construction for all birds
rationale: The claim is concrete but the data are scattered across species accounts, and the definition of a nest decides the answer. Several other birds lay on bare ground, which would likely refute 'only'.

operationalization: Compare yolk and albumen mass fractions of eggs of waterbirds and land birds, ideally with phylogenetic control; the claim holds if waterbird eggs have a systematically higher yolk fraction.
obstacles: Egg-composition measurements sit in scattered papers
Precocial or altricial development and body size confound habitat
rationale: The variables are standard and one could compile them, but no consolidated open dataset exists. The comparison is confounded by developmental mode, since precocial waterfowl hatch with large yolk reserves.

operationalization: Measure egg shape (elongation, asymmetry) against the molecularly determined sex of the chick, in domestic fowl and other species, and test whether egg shape predicts sex.

candidate_datasets.name: Avian egg shape: form, function, and evolution (Stoddard et al. 2017 dataset)
candidate_datasets.role: egg shape indices for thousands of species, without chick sex

obstacles: Shape data and sex data are rarely recorded for the same eggs
Egg shape varies strongly with hen age and breed
rationale: Egg shape is well measured across species, but pairing it with sex needs data from individual-egg studies in poultry science that are not pooled. A negative result in published studies is likely.

operationalization: Check whether hens kept without any male lay eggs, and whether those eggs are infertile; if so wind-eggs arise without prior copulation.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts of fowl and goose reproduction and egg laying

obstacles: The claim is about the origin of unfertilised eggs, which is established in poultry production rather than in a named dataset
rationale: Egg-laying by unmated hens is a basic fact of poultry biology and is confirmed by production records. The test clearly rejects the rival view that such eggs are residue of earlier mating.

operationalization: Regress incubation period and the time from copulation to laying on parent body mass across bird species; the claim holds if both rise with size.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: incubation time and body mass for many bird species

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET: morphological, ecological and geographical data for all birds
candidate_datasets.role: body mass for birds

obstacles: Copulation-to-laying intervals are not tabulated for many species
Phylogenetic non-independence must be handled
rationale: Incubation time against body mass is a standard allometry. The copulation-to-egg interval is poorly covered, so the claim is tested mainly through the incubation component.

operationalization: Compare the stage at which the heart tube becomes visible and starts beating in the chick embryo with the descriptions of the heart appearing as a beating blood speck.

candidate_datasets.name: Hamburger and Hamilton (1951) series of the chick embryo
candidate_datasets.role: standard staging of chick development, including heart formation and the first heartbeat

obstacles: 'Speck of blood' is a visual description to match with a tube forming from the mesoderm
rationale: Chick embryology is documented in detail, so the description can be matched directly. The claim is a rare case where an ancient observation can be confirmed.

operationalization: Use nest-monitoring studies of eagles to measure how often a second chick is lost and whether the mother or a sibling is responsible; the claim fails if the loss is caused by the sibling rather than the parent.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: eagle breeding accounts describing brood reduction and siblicide

obstacles: Modern studies attribute chick loss to siblicide by the older chick rather than expulsion by the mother
Observations are species-specific and mostly in papers
rationale: Brood reduction in eagles is well studied, so the facts exist, but they are in individual studies. The mechanism Aristotle names, maternal expulsion, differs from the usual modern account, which lowers resolution of the claim as stated.

operationalization: Look up the clutch size of the raven; the claim is confirmed if the typical clutch exceeds two.

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote Life-History Database
candidate_datasets.role: clutch size for Corvus corax

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: raven breeding account

rationale: Clutch size for the raven is documented and the claim is a simple threshold on one species. Existing data settle it in minutes.

operationalization: Compile cuckoo host species and test whether the laying female removes host eggs, and whether doves are favoured hosts; hosts being mostly small passerines rather than pigeons would refute part of the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: cuckoo breeding account listing hosts and egg-removal behaviour

obstacles: Host records are scattered across regional studies
Aristotle's 'ringdove' and 'hypolais' names need mapping to species
rationale: Brood parasitism by the cuckoo is well documented, and egg removal is a known behaviour. The preference for ringdove nests is the part least likely to hold, and host data are not pooled in one dataset.

operationalization: Tabulate reproductive mode for cartilaginous fishes and other fishes; the claim is refuted by oviparous sharks and rays and by viviparous bony fishes.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode for fish species, including live-bearing teleosts

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia: a database of shark and ray life-history traits
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode for sharks and rays

obstacles: Oviparity, ovoviviparity and placental viviparity must be separated
rationale: Reproductive mode is recorded for most sharks, rays and bony fishes. The data clearly discriminate the claim, since many skates and sharks lay eggs and some teleosts bear live young.

operationalization: Check the primary literature for a yolk-sac placenta in the species Aristotle calls the smooth shark (Mustelus); the claim holds if embryos attach to the uterus by a umbilical stalk and are nourished through it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode and species accounts for Mustelus

obstacles: The mapping of 'smooth shark' to Mustelus species is uncertain
Data are in anatomical papers, not a trait database
rationale: Placental viviparity in Mustelus is documented in the shark literature, so the claim can be assessed, but one has to compile it from papers and pick the species.

operationalization: Record the sex of each embryo and the uterine horn it occupies in pregnant smooth hounds; a lateral sex bias would confirm the claim and a random distribution would refute it.
obstacles: No dataset links embryo sex to uterine side
Needs dissections of pregnant sharks from fisheries sampling
rationale: The test is simple and decisive, but no existing dataset is known to record embryo position by sex. It would need new data from fisheries-bycatch dissections.

operationalization: Tabulate reproductive mode for scaled fishes (teleosts) and test whether any are live-bearing; a single live-bearing scaly fish refutes 'all'.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode of teleost species, including live-bearers

obstacles: Aristotle's group of 'scaly fish' and 'smooth fish' must be mapped to modern taxa
rationale: Live-bearing teleosts with scales, such as poeciliids and many rockfishes, are well recorded. A universal claim over a well-surveyed group is easy to refute.

operationalization: Compare fertilisation rates in spawned eggs that were reached by milt with those that were not, and confirm that males release milt after females lay; this is documented spawning behaviour for many fishes.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: spawning behaviour and fertilisation mode for fish species

obstacles: The claim is mostly established textbook biology for external fertilisers
It does not hold for internally fertilising fishes
rationale: External fertilisation in teleosts is well established, but the claim's wording about fertile and infertile eggs needs interpretation, and not all fishes spawn this way.

operationalization: List fish species with male or female egg-guarding behaviour; the claim is refuted if more than the sheat-fish and the carp guard their eggs.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive guild and parental care for fish species

obstacles: Parental care categories differ between sources
rationale: Parental care in fishes is widely recorded and many species guard their eggs, such as sticklebacks, gobies and cichlids. The 'only' claim is therefore easy to refute.

operationalization: Check whether eels in the wild have gonads, milt or ovaries, and when; histology of yellow and silver eels would confirm or refute the absence of reproductive organs.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Anguilla life-history and reproduction accounts

obstacles: Gonads are present but undeveloped in yellow eels and mature during the silver-eel migration
Wild spawning was not observed until recently
rationale: Eel gonad development is well studied and shows that eels do have gonads and spawn in the Sargasso Sea, so the claim as stated can be refuted. The data sit in papers rather than in a single repository.

operationalization: Examine how small fishes reappear in dried ponds after rain and whether eggs are present; resistant eggs hatching would explain the observation without spontaneous generation.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: life-history accounts for annual killifish and other fishes of temporary waters

obstacles: The claim names no specific species
Only the observable consequence, not spontaneous generation itself, can be tested
rationale: Spontaneous generation is refuted by the known biology of eggs resistant to drought, but the claim's own observation is only partly tied to datasets. Only the observable part is testable.

operationalization: Compile gestation or egg-carrying durations for fish species and test whether they are multiples of seven days; a distribution of durations without such structure refutes the claim.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: egg development and spawning durations for some species

obstacles: Durations are reported as ranges, never to the day
Gestation in fishes is poorly defined for egg-laying species
rationale: The numeric claim is highly falsifiable, but durations are not recorded with the precision needed, and temperature changes them. Test data cover only a subset of species.

operationalization: Compare fecundity of sharks and rays with that of teleosts and test whether lower fecundity coincides with live-bearing and larger young across species.

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia: a database of shark and ray life-history traits
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and life-history traits of sharks and rays

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fecundity for teleosts

obstacles: The causal explanation is confounded by body size and lifestyle
Viviparity is itself correlated with other traits
rationale: The fecundity difference is easy to check, but the explanation can only be tested through correlations across species, which are confounded.

operationalization: Check the reproductive mode of cetacean species; the claim is confirmed if every cetacean gives birth to live young.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA: species-level mammal life-history, ecology and geography
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive traits of cetacean species

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: reproduction and longevity of cetaceans

rationale: Live birth in cetaceans is established and recorded for essentially all species. The claim is a universal over a small group and is directly checkable.

operationalization: Compare reported gestation length of the common dolphin with ten months.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA: species-level mammal life-history, ecology and geography
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length for dolphin species

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation and longevity for dolphins

obstacles: Aristotle's 'dolphin' maps to the common dolphin or bottlenose dolphin
rationale: Gestation length is a standard trait recorded for the relevant species. A value of 10 to 12 months is the usual range, so the claim can be confirmed or refuted easily.

operationalization: Score aggression by sex and reproductive state across mammal species; no existing source codes irritability this way, so a new cross-species ethogram review would be required.
obstacles: 'Cross-tempered' is subjective
No database codes aggression by reproductive state
rationale: Rut aggression in males is well known and maternal aggression is documented too, but no dataset allows the cross-species claim to be tested as stated.

operationalization: Track estrus mares in the wild and test whether their flight direction is limited to the north-south axis; the claim is refuted by any flight in other directions.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank animal tracking data repository
candidate_datasets.role: GPS tracks of free-ranging horses that could be searched for movements

obstacles: Tracks do not flag estrus
Horses in the data are managed, not wild
rationale: The prediction is crisp, but the data needed, directions of travel of mares in heat, are not in existing repositories. New observations or tracking linked with reproductive state would be needed.

operationalization: Link lamb and kid sex ratios from flock records to the wind direction at mating from weather reanalysis; the claim holds if there is a north versus south difference.

candidate_datasets.name: Copernicus Climate Data Store (ERA5 reanalysis wind data)
candidate_datasets.role: historical wind direction at flock locations and dates

obstacles: Mating dates and flock locations are rarely published
Effects of other factors on sex ratio are large
rationale: Wind data exist globally and livestock sex ratios are recorded, but the two have to be linked via mating dates that are not generally available. Published sex-ratio studies make a negative result likely.

operationalization: Compare reported dog gestation (about 63 days) and the age at eye opening with sixty days and twelve days.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: dog gestation length

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA: species-level mammal life-history, ecology and geography
candidate_datasets.role: dog gestation length and litter size

obstacles: 'Laconian hound' maps to no modern breed
Breed differences in gestation are small
rationale: Dog gestation and eye-opening are well documented, so the numbers can be compared. The breed cannot be matched to a modern one, so the claim is resolved only for dogs in general.

operationalization: Check the dog's dental eruption schedule: whether all deciduous teeth, and not only the canines, are replaced and when.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts describing dentition

rationale: Dog dentition is documented in veterinary and zoological references. The claim is unambiguous and can be refuted by standard knowledge of deciduous teeth.

operationalization: Compare cattle gestation length (about 283 days) with nine months.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: cattle gestation length

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA: species-level mammal life-history, ecology and geography
candidate_datasets.role: cattle gestation length

rationale: Gestation length of cattle is recorded in several databases and the claim is a numerical comparison. Existing data would confirm it closely.

operationalization: Analyse neonatal survival of calves born at different days before term in veterinary and dairy records; any calf that survives after early birth refutes the claim.
obstacles: Survival depends on the degree of prematurity and on veterinary care
Records are held by herd-management and veterinary sources
rationale: Premature calves can survive, and veterinary studies document the gradient, but no open dataset is known. A single documented survivor already refutes the universal claim.

operationalization: Compare the schedule of equine tooth eruption with sets of four at 2.5, 3.5 and 4.5 years and none after.
obstacles: Schedules are in veterinary textbooks and not in an open dataset
Individual and breed variation in timing
rationale: The ageing of horses by teeth is a standard veterinary method with a well-known schedule, so the claim can be checked. It sits in reference books rather than a repository.

operationalization: Score birthing posture of mares and of other quadrupeds in foaling records and obstetric references; the claim fails if mares usually lie down to foal or other quadrupeds also stand.
obstacles: Observational data are not pooled
Posture varies between individuals
rationale: Equine obstetrics sources describe maternal posture at foaling, and mares are often recumbent, but no dataset compares postures across quadrupeds.

operationalization: Compare gestation length of mules and hinnies with the species norms of the sire and of the dam; the claim holds if it matches the sire's.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: gestation lengths of the horse and the donkey as the parent norms

obstacles: Mule gestation data are in breeding records and veterinary papers
Sample sizes are small for hinnies
rationale: Parent-species gestation norms exist, but hybrid gestation records are scattered. The discriminating test is feasible with a compiled sample.

operationalization: Count documented mule pregnancies and how many reached term, from case reports; some fertile mules are known, which confirms the existence of exceptions.
obstacles: The claim combines a general statement with a local exception
Case reports are not pooled
rationale: Case reports of fertile mules exist and are rare, so the broad claim can be assessed, but the Syrian exception cannot be checked.

operationalization: Compare elephant gestation (about 22 months) with the claimed 30 to 36 months.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: elephant gestation length

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA: species-level mammal life-history, ecology and geography
candidate_datasets.role: elephant gestation length

rationale: Elephant gestation is well recorded, and a value near 22 months would refute the stated range. The test is a direct numerical comparison.

operationalization: Check descriptions of elephant calf behaviour for how the calf nurses and how soon it walks; the claim holds if calves nurse with the mouth and walk within hours.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: elephant species accounts describing nursing and neonatal development

obstacles: Details sit in species accounts and field studies
rationale: Calf nursing and early mobility in elephants are well described in the husbandry and field literature, so the claim is directly checkable.

operationalization: Compare deer maximum longevity with other mammals, and check whether short gestation and fast growth predict short lifespan across mammals.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity and growth data for deer and other mammals

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA: species-level mammal life-history, ecology and geography
candidate_datasets.role: gestation length and body size for deer

obstacles: The inference from gestation to lifespan is a correlation, not a rule
'Extreme longevity' needs a threshold
rationale: Longevity and gestation data exist for deer and other mammals, so the conclusion and the inference can be evaluated. The mechanism part of the claim is only a correlation.

operationalization: Compare the gestation of bears, including delayed implantation, with thirty days.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: bear gestation length

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA: species-level mammal life-history, ecology and geography
candidate_datasets.role: bear gestation length

obstacles: Delayed implantation makes 'gestation' definition-dependent
rationale: Bear gestation is documented. Total pregnancy is about six to nine months, though active embryonic development lasts only a few weeks, so the claim's reading matters but the data are clear.

operationalization: Compute neonate mass divided by adult female mass for mammals and check whether the bear cub is the smallest ratio; marsupials such as the giant kangaroo would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA: species-level mammal life-history, ecology and geography
candidate_datasets.role: neonate body mass and adult body mass for mammals

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: birth weight and adult weight

obstacles: Marsupial neonates are far smaller proportionally
'Of all animals' needs a restriction to a defined group
rationale: Neonate and adult mass are recorded for many mammals, so the ratio is easy to compute. The universal 'of all animals' is checkable only for the taxa covered.

operationalization: Compile historical and fossil records of lions in Europe by region and period and see whether their historic range was limited to the Balkan strip between the two rivers.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences of Panthera leo in Europe

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence records including museum specimens

obstacles: The claim concerns a specific historical period for which records are sparse
Fossil and historical records are of unequal quality
rationale: Fossil and historical sources bear on the lion's former range, but the data are sparse and are chiefly written. The claim can be tested only by proxy.

operationalization: Check anatomical studies of the female spotted hyena's external genitalia for a urogenital canal and for the presence of a uterus; the claim fails if the false organ has a duct.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource: 3D specimen scans
candidate_datasets.role: 3D scans of hyena specimens

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biodiversity Information Facility
candidate_datasets.role: specimen records to identify hyena species

obstacles: 'Hyena' could refer to the spotted, striped or brown hyena
Data are in anatomical papers
rationale: The spotted hyena's pseudo-penis is traversed by the urogenital canal, so a duct is present. Anatomical papers settle this, though the species mapping needs checking.

operationalization: Check whether hares breed year-round, show superfetation and give birth monthly in studies of lagomorph reproduction.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA: species-level mammal life-history, ecology and geography
candidate_datasets.role: litters per year and reproductive traits for hares

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: hare species accounts

obstacles: Breeding seasons vary by species and latitude
Superfetation is documented in a few species only
rationale: Hares are known to show superfetation, and some breed through most of the year, but 'every month' and 'all seasons' need qualification. Lagomorph literature is sufficient for a partial test.

operationalization: Check whether hare young are born with open eyes; leverets are precocial and born furred and sighted, which refutes the claim for hares.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: hare species accounts describing leverets at birth

rationale: Hare development is described in standard references. Because the young are born with their eyes open, the claim is cleanly refutable.

operationalization: Combine gestation, litter size and time to maturity of the house mouse to compute the maximum number of mice one pregnant female can produce in the described interval; over 120 in days or weeks is impossible.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: mouse gestation, litter size and maturity

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA: species-level mammal life-history, ecology and geography
candidate_datasets.role: mouse litter size and gestation length

obstacles: 'A little while' is not specified
The report is a single anecdote
rationale: Mouse reproductive parameters are well documented, so the arithmetic is easy and shows the stated number requires many weeks. The vagueness of the time reduces operationalizability.
